paragraphs: When training data comes from several sources, a fixed collection budget creates a practical choice: which source should supply the next example? This paper makes that choice part of learning itself. At each round, its algorithm selects a source, collects and annotates data, and updates the model, aiming to minimize expected loss across the sources.

The method, UCB-OGD, combines upper-confidence-bound sampling with online gradient descent. The sampling component uses uncertainty to guide source selection, while the optimization component updates the model from the collected evidence. Connecting these decisions lets data collection adapt as training proceeds, rather than committing the entire budget to a fixed allocation beforehand.

The authors prove a minimax regret bound of O(sqrt(T K ln T)) for K sources over T rounds, with a lower bound establishing optimality up to a logarithmic factor. Evaluations on standard datasets and smart-city intersection object detection report consistent improvements over random sampling and several active learning methods. Together, these results support adaptive source selection both theoretically and empirically.
icml-2025-adaptive-data-collection-for-r.tldr: UCB-OGD adaptively chooses data sources during training, improving reported performance under a fixed collection budget with near-optimal regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Selecting a model configuration involves more than finding a promising score: the chosen configuration may also need a statistical guarantee about its population risk. Adaptive learn-then-test, or aLTT, addresses this selection problem while trying to reduce the amount of testing required. Its guarantees apply with a finite number of observations.

Existing learn-then-test uses multiple hypothesis testing based on conventional p-values. The proposed method instead uses e-processes to support sequential, data-dependent testing with early termination. This allows the testing procedure to respond to accumulating evidence and stop early while preserving statistical validity. The central contribution is therefore a way to make testing adaptive without giving up the stated risk guarantees.

The paper demonstrates the approach in online policy selection for offline reinforcement learning and in prompt engineering. In these applications, aLTT reaches the same performance as LTT using only a fraction of the testing rounds. That reduction is particularly relevant when each additional test is expensive or exposes a system to safety risks, because the selection procedure itself consumes resources.
icml-2025-adaptive-learn-then-test-stati.tldr: Adaptive learn-then-test preserves finite-sample risk guarantees while reducing testing rounds through sequential testing and early stopping.

paragraphs: Image-to-image diffusion systems respond to both an input image and a text prompt. This paper investigates a safety vulnerability in the image input: changing that image can induce the generation of unsafe content even when the text prompt stays unchanged. This broadens the attack surface beyond adversarial wording, which text-based filters can often detect.

The proposed framework, AdvI2I, trains a generator to produce adversarial input images. The authors report that these images can bypass defenses including Safe Latent Diffusion. An extended version, AdvI2I-Adaptive, accounts for potential countermeasures and reduces resemblance between adversarial images and representations of unsafe concepts. Its purpose is to make the attack more resistant to defenses aimed at recognizing those concepts.

Experiments show that both versions can circumvent the evaluated safeguards. The finding is significant because screening or constraining the text channel does not fully address the behavior induced by image inputs. The work provides empirical evidence that safety measures for image-to-image generation need to account for adversarial visual conditioning as well as prompts.
icml-2025-advi2i-adversarial-image-attac.tldr: AdvI2I shows that manipulated input images can bypass evaluated image-to-image diffusion safeguards without changing the text prompt.

paragraphs: Editing a CAD model from a written instruction requires understanding both the requested change and the design that already exists. The paper introduces CAD-Editor to address this task. It targets a gap in earlier approaches, which concentrate on generating design variations or producing CAD from text without adequately combining textual control with an existing model.

One obstacle is obtaining aligned training examples containing an original model, an edited model, and an instruction describing the change. CAD-Editor creates these triplets automatically. Design variation models supply paired designs, and large vision-language models turn their differences into editing instructions. This connects the generated instruction directly to a concrete before-and-after example.

The editing system then separates the work into locating the regions that need modification and filling those regions with the requested edits. Large language models support both stages through language understanding and CAD knowledge. Experiments report superior quantitative and qualitative performance. The contribution brings together a source of training supervision and a task decomposition tailored to modifying an existing design.
icml-2025-cad-editor-a-locate-then-infil.tldr: CAD-Editor synthesizes editing examples and uses language models to locate and fill requested changes in existing CAD designs.

paragraphs: One-shot federated learning reduces communication by replacing repeated exchanges with a single round of local model uploads. The paper identifies a problem with that saving: independently trained client models can disagree in their feature representations and predictions. Its theoretical and empirical analysis links this inconsistency to degradation in the resulting global model.

FAFI addresses the issue during client training. It combines unsupervised feature alignment with category-wise prototype learning so that clients represent their local samples more consistently. Prototypes provide category-level representations, while feature alignment targets disagreement in the features themselves. The approach therefore tries to improve the compatibility of what clients upload before global inference takes place.

For global inference, FAFI fuses features according to their informativeness and aggregates the learned prototypes. Experiments on three datasets report better performance than 11 one-shot federated learning baselines, including a reported accuracy gain of 10.86%. The results support the paper's central argument that the quality and consistency of local training are important to making a single communication round effective.
icml-2025-does-one-shot-give-the-best-sh.tldr: FAFI improves one-shot federated learning by aligning client representations before combining their features and category prototypes.

paragraphs: Long-context fine-tuning datasets often contain many short sequences and relatively few long ones. Training strategies designed around long sequences can use this mixture inefficiently. Unequal sequence lengths also create uneven work across devices and idle gaps in pipeline execution, reducing GPU utilization even when substantial computation remains to be done.

ChunkFlow reorganizes training around uniformly sized chunks. It combines short sequences and splits long sequences so that the units being scheduled are more balanced. A state-aware scheduler then manages these chunks so that peak memory usage depends primarily on chunk size rather than the longest sequence in the dataset. The scheduler can also work with existing pipeline scheduling algorithms.

Experiments report speedups of up to 4.53 times over Megatron-LM for long-context fine-tuning. This is a best reported speedup, rather than a uniform improvement across all settings. The authors also suggest that the approach could help with long-context continual pre-training and other workloads containing variable-length sequences. The practical insight is to organize computation around balanced work units while accounting for their memory state.
icml-2025-efficient-long-context-fine-tu.tldr: ChunkFlow balances variable-length training data into scheduled chunks, delivering reported fine-tuning speedups of up to 4.53 times over Megatron-LM.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models divide processing among specialized components, making the routing decision central to how those components are used. This paper applies that idea to diffusion transformers for visual generation. Its model, Race-DiT, introduces an Expert Race routing strategy intended to make expert assignment more flexible as the model scales.

Expert Race lets tokens and experts compete together, selecting the strongest candidates for assignment. This allows the model to learn dynamic allocations of experts to critical tokens. The design focuses on matching processing resources to the tokens that need them, rather than treating expert selection as a separate fixed pattern across all inputs.

The authors also introduce per-layer regularization to address difficulties learning in shallow layers, plus a router similarity loss to counter mode collapse and improve expert utilization. Experiments on ImageNet report significant performance gains and promising scaling behavior. The findings support the combined routing and regularization design as an effective way to use expert capacity in diffusion transformers on the evaluated image-generation setting.
icml-2025-expert-race-a-flexible-routing.tldr: Race-DiT dynamically matches tokens with experts and adds routing regularization, producing reported ImageNet gains with promising scaling behavior.

paragraphs: An agent can sometimes solve a task successfully yet perform inconsistently across repeated attempts. Guided search tries to improve average performance by examining alternative solution paths. However, methods such as Monte Carlo tree search become difficult to use when intermediate environment states cannot easily be saved and restored, as in the software environments studied here.

The paper investigates two complementary options for this setting: one-step lookahead and trajectory selection. Both use a learned action-value estimator to guide choices toward promising outcomes. One considers a nearby decision, while the other selects among trajectories. These strategies make guided search applicable where repeatedly branching from saved environment states is impractical.

On SWE-bench Verified, the methods double the average success rate of a fine-tuned Qwen-72B model to 40.8%, reported as a new state of the art for open-weights models in the paper. Similar improvements transfer to GPT-4o. These results suggest that value-guided selection can recover more of an agent's demonstrated capability even when its operating environment restricts conventional search.
icml-2025-guided-search-strategies-in-no.tldr: Value-guided lookahead and trajectory selection improve software agents in environments where saving and restoring intermediate states is difficult.

paragraphs: Learning to solve partial differential equations requires capturing both local variation and structure across an entire domain. The paper describes a split between attention-based methods, which adapt at individual points, and spectral methods, which supply continuity priors across the domain. Each approach offers something useful, but its counterpart's strengths are difficult to reproduce within the same design.

Holistic Physics Mixer, or HPM, brings spectral and physical information into a shared framework. Attention-based and spectral-based approaches appear as special cases, while the broader formulation permits interactions between the two kinds of information. The intended benefit is a solver that combines local flexibility with the generalization properties associated with spectral structure.

Across diverse PDE experiments, HPM reportedly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and computational efficiency. It also shows strong generalization with limited training data and zero-shot performance at resolutions not encountered during training. These findings support the value of integrating the two representations: the reported improvements concern both solution quality and the ability to apply learned behavior beyond the training resolution.
icml-2025-holistic-physics-solver-learni.tldr: HPM combines spectral structure with point-level adaptability, reporting more accurate and efficient PDE solving plus strong transfer to unseen resolutions.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models can learn from multiple domains and then adapt to a target task through prompting. BRIDGE addresses a question behind this workflow: how much source knowledge can usefully transfer? The paper combines a model architecture for selective transfer with a theoretical bound intended to make its generalization behavior more understandable.

During pre-training, domain-invariant aligners bring graph features from different domains into alignment to learn discriminative source knowledge. A lightweight mixture-of-experts network then supports downstream prompting. Through self-supervised selection and assembly, it decides how to combine available knowledge for transfer, giving the model a mechanism for choosing among information learned across domains.

The theoretical analysis uses graph spectral structure and assumes Lipschitz continuity to derive an optimizable upper bound on generalization error. This is a conditional bound, rather than an exact measurement of transfer in every setting. Experiments on node and graph classification report superiority over 15 state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution links selective knowledge transfer with both empirical classification results and a mathematically specified account of generalization.
icml-2025-how-much-can-transfer-bridge-b.tldr: BRIDGE aligns multi-domain graph knowledge and selectively transfers it through experts, with an optimizable generalization bound under Lipschitz continuity.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks learn by passing information between connected nodes, but the paper argues that conventional node representations do not explicitly ensure preservation of graph topology. It proposes viewing message passing as a system of hyperbolic partial differential equations. This turns representation updates into a dynamical process tied to a particular solution space.

That solution space is built from eigenvectors describing the graph's structure. At any time in the system, node features can be expressed as combinations of these basis vectors. This gives the evolving features an explicit connection to topology and provides a way to interpret message passing through the structural components it represents.

Solving the differential-equation system establishes a connection to spectral graph neural networks, yielding a framework for enhancing their message passing. The authors also use polynomials to approximate filter functions within this approach. Experiments across diverse graph tasks report flexibility and significant improvements for several spectral GNNs. The work therefore offers both an interpretable mathematical formulation and an empirically useful enhancement to existing spectral models.
icml-2025-hyperbolic-pde-gnn-spectral-gr.tldr: A hyperbolic-PDE formulation ties graph message passing explicitly to topological eigenvectors and improves tested spectral GNNs.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders seek understandable features inside neural representations while retaining enough information to reconstruct those representations. These goals can compete: using fewer active features can make reconstruction harder. This paper studies that challenge in vision-language models and introduces Matryoshka SAE, or MSAE, to learn representations at multiple levels of detail simultaneously.

The architecture organizes features hierarchically, allowing direct optimization of reconstruction quality and sparsity. For CLIP, the authors report an improved Pareto frontier, meaning better available trade-offs between these objectives. Their reported results include 0.99 cosine similarity and a fraction of unexplained variance below 0.1 while maintaining 80% sparsity, indicating close reconstruction with many inactive features.

The paper also tests whether the extracted features are useful for interpretation and control. MSAE identifies more than 120 semantic concepts and uses them for concept-based similarity search and bias analysis in downstream tasks such as CelebA. These demonstrations connect the representation metrics to practical analysis: the learned components provide concepts through which CLIP's behavior can be examined and influenced.
icml-2025-interpreting-clip-with-hierarc.tldr: Matryoshka SAE learns hierarchical sparse features that closely reconstruct CLIP representations and support concept-based search and bias analysis.

paragraphs: Large-model training depends heavily on optimizers that turn noisy gradient estimates into useful parameter updates. Although variance reduction has a substantial history in stochastic optimization, the paper notes that it has not achieved widespread success in deep-network and language-model training. MARS aims to make this family of techniques effective alongside the adaptive methods already used for these workloads.

The framework combines preconditioned gradient methods with variance reduction through scaled stochastic recursive momentum. Preconditioning changes how gradient updates are scaled, while variance reduction addresses their stochastic variability. MARS brings these functions together in one optimization framework, rather than treating the choice of update geometry and the handling of gradient noise as unrelated decisions.

The authors instantiate the framework with updates based on AdamW, Lion, and Shampoo, and establish connections to existing optimizers. In GPT-2 training experiments, MARS consistently outperforms AdamW by a large margin. The reported finding supports the usefulness of this combination for the tested models and gives several concrete optimizer variants through which the framework can be applied.
icml-2025-mars-unleashing-the-power-of-v.tldr: MARS combines variance reduction with preconditioned updates and consistently outperforms AdamW by a large margin in reported GPT-2 training experiments.

paragraphs: Multi-objective reinforcement learning must accommodate different preferences among conflicting goals. Learning offline avoids extensive new interactions, but collected data may cover only a narrow set of those preferences. MODULI addresses the resulting problem: a policy can behave poorly when asked to follow a preference outside the dataset's coverage.

The method uses a preference-conditioned diffusion model to plan trajectories and derive actions. Two return-normalization methods refine the guidance used during generation. MODULI also trains a slider adapter to capture directions of preference change. Its sliding guidance mechanism moves from preferences represented in the data toward out-of-distribution preferences, helping extend the available set of trade-offs.

The paper describes this as filling gaps in and extending an incomplete Pareto front, the collection of competing objective trade-offs. On the D4MORL benchmark, MODULI outperforms state-of-the-art offline multi-objective reinforcement learning baselines and shows strong generalization to unseen preference regions. The results support guided diffusion planning as a way to produce behavior better aligned with requested trade-offs beyond those well represented in the offline data.
icml-2025-moduli-unlocking-preference-ge.tldr: MODULI uses preference-conditioned diffusion planning and sliding guidance to improve offline reinforcement learning for preferences outside the training data's coverage.

paragraphs: An explanation of a time-series prediction can fail by including irrelevant patterns or by leaving out important ones. This paper treats those failures as linked optimization problems. Its Optimal Information Retention Principle uses conditional mutual information to formalize the goals of reducing redundancy and retaining a complete account of the relevant information.

The authors derive an objective from that principle and build ORTE, a practical explanation framework. ORTE learns a binary mask that filters the time series while capturing temporal patterns useful for explanation. The mask makes the selection explicit: information is either retained or removed according to the learned explanation process.

Training combines a decoupled discrete mapping process, intended to keep gradient propagation stable, with contrastive learning to sharpen pattern filtering. The resulting framework balances low redundancy against high completeness. Quantitative and qualitative experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report improved explanation accuracy and completeness over baseline methods. The contribution is a common information-based criterion connecting what an explanation should preserve to how its mask is learned.
icml-2025-optimal-information-retention-.tldr: ORTE learns time-series explanation masks using an information-based objective that balances removing irrelevant patterns with retaining important ones.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets of possible answers with coverage guarantees. Many methods reserve separate data for parameter tuning and calibration to preserve the exchangeability assumption behind those guarantees. This paper studies what happens when the same data serves both purposes, focusing on the resulting coverage gap, which it calls tuning bias.

The authors empirically find that this bias is negligible for simple parameter tuning in many conformal prediction methods. They also observe a scaling relationship: bias grows with the complexity of the parameter space and shrinks as the calibration dataset becomes larger. This connects the consequences of data reuse to both tuning flexibility and available sample size.

The paper develops a theoretical framework and derives an upper bound that rigorously supports the scaling law. It then discusses ways to reduce tuning bias using that theory. The findings give a more quantitative account of when reuse may have a small coverage effect. They do not make the empirical observation of negligible bias a universal guarantee for arbitrary tuning complexity or calibration size.
icml-2025-parametric-scaling-law-of-tuni.tldr: The paper bounds coverage bias from reusing conformal calibration data for tuning, linking greater bias to parameter complexity and smaller datasets.

paragraphs: Black-box optimization searches for good inputs when the objective function must be evaluated rather than directly analyzed. High-dimensional problems make this search difficult, and Bayesian optimization can struggle with both dimensionality and large evaluation histories. DiBO combines generative modeling with uncertainty estimation to guide candidate selection in this setting.

The framework repeatedly alternates between two stages. First, a diffusion model learns the data distribution, while deep ensembles predict objective values and quantify uncertainty. Second, candidate selection becomes a posterior inference problem. This formulation balances exploitation of inputs that appear promising with exploration of regions where predictions remain uncertain.

DiBO fine-tunes its diffusion model to amortize posterior inference, placing the work of learning to generate candidates into the model. The design addresses both the expressiveness of the candidate generator and the uncertainty information needed to direct search. Experiments across synthetic and real-world tasks report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. These results support coupling diffusion generation with uncertainty-aware selection for the evaluated high-dimensional optimization problems.
icml-2025-posterior-inference-with-diffu.tldr: DiBO combines diffusion generation with ensemble uncertainty estimates to select promising candidates for high-dimensional black-box optimization.

paragraphs: Protein structure tokenizers turn three-dimensional structures into representations that language-style and multimodal models can process. Comparing these tokenizers is difficult without a shared evaluation framework. StructTokenBench addresses this by assessing quality and efficiency with particular attention to local substructures, complementing evaluations centered on the global shape of a protein.

The benchmark finds that no tokenizer leads across every evaluation perspective. It also reveals underuse of codebooks, the collections of representations available to encode structure. Motivated by that observation, the authors introduce AminoAseed. The strategy improves gradient updates to codebook entries and balances codebook size with representation dimension to improve utilization and tokenizer quality.

Compared with ESM3, AminoAseed reports an average 6.31% performance improvement across 24 supervised tasks, alongside increases of 12.83% in sensitivity and 124.03% in utilization. These measurements connect a diagnosed representation problem to downstream performance gains. The paper contributes both a more detailed evaluation lens and a specific training strategy, while its benchmark finding emphasizes that tokenizer quality has several distinct dimensions.
icml-2025-protein-structure-tokenization.tldr: StructTokenBench exposes trade-offs in protein tokenizers, and AminoAseed improves codebook use with reported gains across 24 supervised tasks.

paragraphs: In some decision problems, the constraints an agent should obey are not written down and must be inferred from expert behavior. Inverse constrained reinforcement learning tackles this task using interactions with an environment. This paper asks how those interactions should be chosen so that learning the constraints is sample-efficient and has a theoretical foundation.

The authors define a feasible cost set and analyze how errors in estimated environment transitions and the expert policy affect the feasibility of inferred constraints. This identifies the uncertainty that exploration needs to reduce. The analysis connects imperfect observations of behavior and dynamics to the reliability of the constraint-learning process.

Two algorithms follow from this framework. One dynamically reduces a bound on aggregate cost-estimation error; the other restricts exploration to policies around those that remain plausibly optimal. Both receive tractable sample-complexity guarantees, and experiments across several environments validate their performance. The contribution makes exploration an explicit part of inverse constraint inference, with mathematical guidance about the amount and direction of sampling needed.
icml-2025-provably-efficient-exploration.tldr: The paper develops two exploration algorithms with sample-complexity guarantees for efficiently inferring constraints from expert behavior.

paragraphs: Language models usually learn to predict tokens through cross-entropy, which treats alternative tokens as categories. For numbers, that objective does not express how close a predicted value is to the correct one. The paper introduces Number Token Loss, or NTL, to add numerical proximity directly to training while keeping predictions at the token level.

NTL has two variants, based on an Lp norm or a Wasserstein distance between the numerical values associated with target and predicted number tokens. It supplements the existing cross-entropy objective and can be added without runtime overhead. This gives training a numerical signal while retaining the language model's ordinary token-generation interface.

Across mathematical datasets, the authors report consistent improvements on math-related tasks. In a direct regression comparison, NTL matches the performance of a regression head despite operating on tokens. Experiments also show improved performance when scaling to models with three billion parameters. These findings support the possibility of improving quantitative behavior through the training objective itself, without requiring a separate numerical output mechanism.
icml-2025-regress-dont-guess-a-regressio.tldr: Number Token Loss adds numerical proximity to language-model training and improves reported mathematical performance without runtime overhead.

paragraphs: Repeatedly checking and revising an answer can improve language-model reasoning, but the feedback and revision roles need to work together. The paper argues that existing approaches restrict feedback or train the participating components without sufficient coordination. It models multi-turn refinement as a Markov decision process so that the sequence of revisions becomes a learning problem.

Its algorithm, DPSDP, trains an actor-critic language-model system through direct preference learning on self-generated data. The actor and critic participate in iterative answer refinement, with dynamic programming guiding policy search. The theoretical result states that DPSDP can match any policy within the training distribution, making the scope of that guarantee explicitly distribution-dependent.

Experiments with several base models show improvements on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks. For Ministral-based models on MATH 500, majority voting across five refinement steps raises accuracy from a first-turn 58.2% to 63.2%. An ablation study supports the benefits of collaboration and out-of-distribution generalization. The empirical results extend the evidence beyond the domain covered by the stated theoretical guarantee.
icml-2025-reinforce-llm-reasoning-throug.tldr: DPSDP jointly trains an actor-critic language-model system to refine answers, with reported reasoning gains inside and outside the training distribution.

paragraphs: Generating a protein backbone requires constructing a coherent three-dimensional arrangement along a chain. Existing diffusion and flow methods can be computationally expensive and produce structures with undesirable designability. ReQFlow addresses both concerns through a flow-matching approach that generates a local position and rotation for each residue from random noise.

The method represents each three-dimensional rotation as a unit quaternion. It constructs rotational flows using spherical linear interpolation in an exponential form, and trains them through quaternion flow matching with a stated numerical-stability guarantee. A subsequent rectification step accelerates inference and improves the designability of the generated backbones, producing the final ReQFlow model.

Experiments report comparable backbone-generation performance with substantially fewer sampling steps and less inference time. For a backbone of length 300, ReQFlow is reported to be 37 times faster than RFDiffusion and 63 times faster than Genie2. Those figures describe the stated example. The broader finding is that the rotation representation and flow rectification can substantially reduce generation cost while retaining competitive output quality.
icml-2025-reqflow-rectified-quaternion-f.tldr: ReQFlow uses rectified quaternion flows to generate competitive protein backbones with fewer sampling steps and substantially faster reported inference.

paragraphs: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent trains models through distributed optimization. This paper studies how well its learned models generalize by analyzing algorithmic stability: how sensitive learning is to changes in the training data. The analysis covers both smooth and nonsmooth problems, with different results for these settings.

For convex, smooth problems, the authors derive stability bounds that depend on training error. This makes progress in optimization relevant to the generalization guarantee. Their bounds remove the Lipschitzness assumption used in earlier results and imply fast rates under a low-noise condition. The condition matters: the faster rates are tied to that setting rather than asserted for every problem.

For nonsmooth problems, the paper establishes what it describes as the first optimal stability-based generalization bounds for decentralized SGD. Additional optimization-error bounds imply minimax-optimal excess-risk rates. The proof combines an error decomposition that uses co-coercivity with control of a neighboring-consensus error. Together, these results sharpen the theoretical connection between optimization, stability, and prediction quality in decentralized training.
icml-2025-stability-and-generalization-a.tldr: Sharper stability analysis gives decentralized SGD improved smooth-problem guarantees and optimal bounds for nonsmooth problems.

paragraphs: Feature selection chooses which measured attributes to use for classification. This paper addresses data where examples within a single class are distributed unevenly or form several dense groups. In these settings, outliers can be genuine examples with patterns relevant to classification, making it important—and difficult—to identify the main body of each class.

The authors propose SIOFS, a supervised feature selection method that focuses on what they call stray intrusive outliers. It modifies a skewness coefficient, which describes distributional asymmetry, and incorporates a threshold from the three-sigma principle to identify the class body. It then scores features according to the outliers’ degree of intrusion.

The method also introduces a refined density-mean center to represent the general characteristics of the class body. Together, these components make the structure within each class central to feature scoring. The authors support their design choices with mathematical formulations, proofs, and logical arguments.

Experiments across 16 diverse benchmark datasets report that SIOFS outperforms 12 state-of-the-art feature selection methods, assessed through classification accuracy, normalized mutual information, and confusion matrices. These findings support the usefulness of accounting for outlier intrusion when selecting features for the class structures studied.
icml-2025-stray-intrusive-outliers-based.tldr: SIOFS selects features using outlier intrusion and within-class structure, reporting better classification results than 12 competing methods across 16 benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: In-context tabular classification aims to adapt to a dataset through supplied examples without training a separate model for each dataset. Methods such as TabPFN perform well on small tables but face scaling difficulties as data becomes larger and more complex. TabFlex targets this bottleneck by replacing quadratic self-attention with linear attention.

The resulting model is designed to accommodate thousands of features, hundreds of classes, and millions of samples. The architectural change addresses the computational growth of attention, enabling the in-context approach to operate at a larger scale. In one reported example, TabFlex processes a poker-hand dataset containing more than a million samples in five seconds.

Across the evaluations, the authors report speedups exceeding two times over TabPFN and 1.5 times over XGBoost, and better efficiency than 25 tested baselines. They also report strong large-dataset performance at reduced computational cost, particularly with dimensionality reduction and data sampling. The findings concern a combination of scalability, efficiency, and predictive effectiveness; the comparison with all 25 baselines is specifically an efficiency result.
icml-2025-tabflex-scaling-tabular-learni.tldr: TabFlex uses linear attention to scale in-context tabular classification to millions of samples with strong reported efficiency.
